Next, we examined the nuclear translocation of actin-associated regulators, YAP and MRTF, by TPM3.1 inhibition in primary chondrocytes. Finally, we determined the effect of YAP and MRTF inhibition on the regulation of chondrogenic and degradative enzyme gene expression in primary chondrocytes. Results: Our results revealed TPM3.1 is present and localized cortically in mouse and bovine chondrocytes. There was a reduction in cortical F-actin staining in Tpm3.1 knockout mouse femoral head cartilage as well as in primary bovine chondrocytes treated with TR100. In primary chondrocytes, TR100 caused a catabolic shift in mRNA levels. This coincided with a decrease in the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio of both YAP and MRTF in TR100-treated cells. Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of either YAP or MRTF partially recapitulated the catabolic shift seen in TR100-treated chondrocytes by a reduction of chondrogenic mRNA levels. Conclusion: Collectively, these results provide insight into the regulation of chondrocyte homeostasis by cortical F-actin stability and the downstream mediators of transcription. A greater understanding of the actin-associated molecules that regulate chondrocyte homeostasis in osteoarthritis may lead to novel insights to target disease progression.

items.title: How thermostats change the thermodynamic, structural and dynamic properties of a Lennard-Jones liquid
items.abstract_or_text: Almost every molecular dynamics simulation is coupled to a thermostat, and every thermostat modifies the equations of motion whose solutions are then interpreted as the physics of the system. The algorithms are well established and their qualitative artefacts are well known, yet a quantitative comparison of the commonly used schemes under one protocol, with the statistical resolution needed to detect their effects, is rarely reported, presumably because such effects are small compared with the run-to-run scatter of a typical simulation. Such a comparison, however, is of practical importance, since it determines which observables a given thermostat can be trusted with. In this work, we compare six temperature-control schemes (windowed velocity rescaling, Berendsen, Nosé–Hoover chains, Langevin, the dissipative-particle-dynamics pair thermostat and canonical sampling through velocity rescaling) at up to four coupling strengths each against an energy-matched microcanonical reference, for the truncated-and-shifted Lennard-Jones liquid, with five independent realizations per case and with finite-size and timestep controls. We find that thermodynamic means and pair structure are the same for all schemes once the mean temperature is matched, whereas the fluctuations differ and the differences propagate into derived quantities such as the heat capacity. For transport, the decisive variable is whether the thermostat acts globally or locally, not how strongly it is coupled: the global schemes leave the self-diffusion coefficient and the viscosity equivalent to those of the microcanonical reference over the whole coupling range, whereas the local stochastic schemes damp diffusion once their friction approaches the intrinsic friction of the liquid. In particular, we show that the Langevin bias at five state points is reproduced to within 16%, with no fitted parameter, by a resistance-addition interpolation whose only input is the cage factor of overdamped Brownian dynamics, and that, once the periodic-box correction is carried over to the screened hydrodynamics of a Langevin liquid, the bath is predicted to remove in the thermodynamic limit a hydrodynamic contribution to diffusion that a finite box conceals. Our results also rationalize two implementation effects in LAMMPS, the kinetic-energy fluctuation deficit of strongly coupled Langevin dynamics and the failure of the stress-autocorrelation viscosity for a strongly coupled pair thermostat, which could otherwise be mistaken for physics. The comparison condenses into simple rules for the choice of a thermostat and its coupling time.

items.title: Anti-GABAB receptor autoimmunity causes cognitive decline by presynaptic pathology
items.abstract_or_text: The GABAB receptor is a central regulator of neuronal transmission and excitability by pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Its dysfunction causes severe neurological disease, but the underlying pathomechanisms remain elusive. Here, we exploit a distinct CNS autoimmune disorder in which patients develop specific autoantibodies against GABAB receptors causing autoimmune encephalitis with severe memory dysfunction and epilepsy. We demonstrate that human autoantibodies target the sushi-domains of the GABAB receptor B1a subunit and the B2 subunit and interfere with presynaptic signaling. This specific presynaptic pathology results from exclusive functional antagonism of the B1a subunit and disrupts short- and long-term synaptic plasticity, abnormally amplifies hippocampal network oscillations and coupling in vivo, and ultimately impairs memory consolidation. Our results demonstrate that autoimmune presynaptic pathomechanisms alone are sufficient to interfere with memory processing, thus defining a causal link between molecular GABAB receptor disturbance, synaptic pathology, circuit dysfunction, and dementia distinct from classical neurodegenerative processes.

items.title: Androgen Receptor SUMO site mutations ameliorate toxicity in Drosophila models of SBMA
items.abstract_or_text: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) is an X-linked neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the androgen receptor (AR) gene that produces a toxic, polyglutamine-expanded protein. SBMA is part of a broader class of polyglutamine (polyQ) diseases characterized by protein misfolding, aggregation, and progressive neuronal dysfunction, for which no disease-modifying therapies exist. Post-translational modification of AR, including SUMOylation, is an important regulator of its transcriptional activity, stability, and cellular localization. Disease protein modification by SUMO is implicated in various neurodegenerative diseases and can influence protein aggregation and toxicity in polyQ disorders. Prior studies suggest that preventing AR SUMOylation positively modifies disease phenotypes. Here, we generated Drosophila models expressing polyQ-expanded human AR in which the canonical SUMO acceptor lysine sites were mutated into arginines to prevent SUMOylation of AR. Using tissue-specific expression in neurons and muscle, we assessed effects on lifespan, motor behavior, AR localization, and gene expression. Mutation of AR SUMOylation sites leads to improvements in longevity when expressed in muscle. Effects on motor performance were more limited. Transcriptomic analysis revealed tissue-specific effects of AR SUMO-site mutation, with enrichment of immune, metabolic, and defense-related processes in heads, but limited enrichment in thoraces. In both tissues, a subset of genes altered by AR SUMO-site mutation showed expression changes opposing those associated with polyQ expansion. These findings support a modulatory role for SUMOylation in SBMA pathogenesis and highlight post-translational regulation of AR as a potential therapeutic avenue requiring further investigation.

items.title: Microglia support regeneration of rod photoreceptors in larval zebrafish retina through Nrf2-independent mechanisms
items.abstract_or_text: The molecular and cellular components of successful regeneration of complex tissues in zebrafish are a major area of investigation. Previous work by our lab indicates a redox function for retinal microglia in the first 48 hours following acute injury to rod photoreceptors in the larval zebrafish retina. In addition, recent literature suggests that microglia provide signals that impact the regenerative response in the damaged retina. Here, we investigate the requirement of microglia and the redox-responsive transcription factor Nrf2 in the spontaneous regeneration of rod photoreceptors in the larval zebrafish retina. We used irf8 mutants which are deficient in microglia, and mutant zebrafish lacking a functional copy of the gene nfe2l2a, which encodes a zebrafish ortholog of Nfe2l2/Nrf2. Our results indicate that microglia support the production of regenerated rods following their ablation. However, although detection of reactive oxygen species was increased in nfe2l2a mutant microglia following rod ablation, the regeneration of rods was not impacted in nfe2l2a mutants. Collectively, our results indicate a role for microglia in supporting the production of regenerated retinal neurons while also indicating that Nrf2-independent mechanisms can likely provide redox functions during rod regeneration.

items.title: Adeno-associated virus serotype tropism and transduction in murine dorsal root ganglia following direct injection.
items.abstract_or_text: The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is highly heterogeneous, comprised of diverse subclasses of motor and sensory neurons. Optogenetics offers a high-resolution approach for interrogating neural circuits; however, optogenetic proteins must be selectively delivered to defined neuronal circuits in order to elucidate circuit-specific functional mechanisms. Adeno-associated viral vectors (AAVs) are widely used to deliver transgenes to the nervous system due to their relative safety and strong transgene expression. Multiple AAV serotypes are in common use, each capable of preferentially transducing distinct tissues and neuronal populations. However, characterization of the transduction behavior of these serotypes in the PNS, particularly in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and sensory nervous system (SNS), remain limited. This study evaluated the transduction efficiency of AAV8, AAV9, AAV2re, and PHP.S following direct intraganglionic injection into the DRG. AAV8, AAV9, and PHP.S exhibited comparable transduction efficiencies, whereas AAV2re transduced more than twofold fewer neurons. Despite similar overall efficiencies between AAV8, AAV9, and PHP.S, the neuronal volume distributions of transduced neurons were serotype-dependent. These results demonstrate that AAV serotype selection influences both the extent and size of transduced DRG neurons, indicating that serotype selection should be considered carefully when designing experiments that target peripheral sensory circuits.

items.title: Chromosome-scale nuclear and mitochondrial genome assemblies reveal extreme genome compartmentalization in the hazelnut pathogen Anisogramma anomala
items.abstract_or_text: Anisogramma anomala is an obligate biotrophic ascomycete and the causal agent of Eastern filbert blight, the most economically important disease of hazelnut in the United States. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale reference genome for A. anomala isolate OR-Ennis-d and characterized its nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture. The 344-Mb nuclear genome was resolved into 9 predicted chromosomes and is repeat-rich, with transposable elements comprising 88.8% of the assembly. Although transposable elements are abundant, their divergence landscape and low retention of conserved protein domains support a history of past extensive transposon proliferation followed by widespread degeneration. Repeat accumulation was highly uneven and generated pronounced genome compartmentalization. Approximately half of predicted genes occur in compact, TE-poor regions with short flanking intergenic regions that are enriched for conserved BUSCO orthologs. In contrast, genes in TE-rich, gene-sparse regions with long flanking intergenic regions are enriched for carbohydrate-active enzymes, secreted proteins, and candidate secreted effector proteins, consistent with a two-speed-like genome architecture. The 462-kb mitochondrial genome is among the largest reported for ascomycetes and contains 117 introns, including an intron adjacent to cob codon 143 that may prevent acquisition of the p.G143A substitution associated with resistance to quinone outside inhibitor fungicides. Finally, we identified mitochondrial DNA insertions at 20 nuclear loci totaling at least 616.9 kb, an unusually extensive amount for a fungal genome. This chromosome-scale genome resource reveals the extreme nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture in A. anomala and provides a foundation for investigating genome evolution and adaptation to hazelnut resistance.

items.title: Aquaporin-4 Regulates Edema, Sustains Astrocyte Differentiation, and Constrains Immunosuppressive Remodeling in Glioblastoma
items.abstract_or_text: Vasogenic cerebral edema is a severe complication that affects most patients with glioblastoma (GBM). It leads to an increase in intracranial pressure, neurological deficits, and increased mortality rates. While there is considerable research on edema formation, the molecular and cellular mechanisms of edema resolution in GBM, particularly in response to dexamethasone or other anti-edema therapies, remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), a key regulator of brain water homeostasis, is upregulated in human GBM compared to the normal brain. AQP4 expression correlates with peritumoral edema in GBM patients, with the classical (CL) GBM subtype exhibiting the highest AQP4 levels but the lowest edema content relative to the proneural (PN) and mesenchymal (MES) subtypes. Using the RCAS/tv-a system, we generated de novo GBM with defined driver mutations in Aqp4-proficient and -deficient mice. Loss of Aqp4 shortened survival and exacerbated edema, accompanied by reduced astrocytic coverage within the tumor core, but not at the tumor margin. Single-cell RNA-sequencing and spatial transcriptomics revealed that Aqp4 loss reprograms astrocytes toward an immature, progenitor-like state and alters their crosstalk with other cell types in the GBM microenvironment. Additionally, loss of Aqp4 skewed myeloid populations toward immunosuppressive phenotypes while reducing lymphoid infiltration. Treatment with anti-VEGFA antibody, an established anti-edema therapy, increased expression of Aqp4 and reduced vessel leakage, underscoring the role of AQP4 in the therapeutic modulation of brain water balance. Overall, this study highlights the important role of AQP4 in resolving edema and its critical function in maintaining astrocyte identity and shaping the immune landscape of GBM.

items.title: ML/MM
items.abstract_or_text: Electrostatic embedding allows a local machine-learning potential to respond to an extended molecular environment without including every environmental atom in its message-passing graph. We construct a fixed-charge machine-learning/molecular-mechanics (ML/MM) interface for the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model. Analytic Gaussian monopole and dipole operators supply the environmental potential, the internal electrostatic features, and the interaction energy. Differentiation through both field-conditioned density updates gives forces on the model fragment and the environment, which are combined with a subtractive classical energy and exact link-atom force redistribution. A reciprocal-space extension treats three-dimensional periodicity at fixed cell. We assess the implementation using fixed-geometry numerical checks and 24 matched QM/MM reference calculations for a 2589-atom rhodopsin model, with 54 atoms in the neural-network graph. The analytic model gives a relative-energy root-mean-square error of 8.62 kJ mol−1 after one constant energy shift, and force-component errors of 0.07345 and 0.00797 eV Å−1 on the 53 real high-level atoms and 2536 environmental atoms, respectively. Analytic operators substantially reduce rotational errors while leaving the QM/MM accuracy essentially unchanged. A nearby water accounts for approximately 74% of the environmental squared force error. Matched charge-density and frozen-density force comparisons identify limitations of both the local multipole representation and its predicted coefficients. The results establish the numerical consistency of the embedding implementation and delimit the single-point accuracy of the transferred pretrained model.

items.title: Role of water in hydrogen-based iron oxide reduction: effects on pore evolution and gas transport
items.abstract_or_text: Hydrogen-based direct reduction offers a low-emission route to ironmaking. Oxygen removal reduces the mass and volume of the solid, creating pores that provide pathways for hydrogen supply and removal of the water produced. Water accumulation within these evolving pores can inhibit further reduction. Here, we develop a phase-field model coupling water generation, transport, and reaction inhibition to pore evolution during wüstite-to-ferrite reduction. The simulations show that water accumulation slows reduction and allows pores to coarsen. Increasing the pore volume fraction accelerates reduction but does not prevent water accumulation when its removal from the pores is limited. Simulating gas diffusion through the resulting fixed pore structures shows that coarser morphologies have higher directional effective diffusivity even at comparable pore fractions. These findings motivate pellet-scale models that account for how reduction history shapes pore morphology and thereby influences gas transport.

items.title: Classic and novel features of the dentate gyrus vascular niche quantified through 3D vessel reconstruction
items.abstract_or_text: Adult neurogenesis, the continued generation of new neurons throughout life, supports a variety of emotional and cognitive functions in mammals. Lifelong neurogenesis occurs in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, where a neurogenic niche supports the survival and growth of neural stem cells (NSCs), which divide to generate new neurons. A key component of this niche is the surrounding vasculature, thought to give NSCs access to circulating support molecules, oxygen, and nutrient metabolites. The DG vasculature is strikingly variable across layers. Vascular density and linearity, for example, have been noted to differ substantially in the different cell layers that make up the DG. Most of these prior descriptions of the DG vasculature have been qualitative, and other important aspects of vessel morphology, like vessel diameter, have not been previously reported to our knowledge. To provide a more complete and quantitative description of the adult DG vasculature, we used a 3D imaging technique to fully characterize the vasculature of each DG cellular layer. Our 3D reconstructions of DG blood vessels provide a quantitative method for measuring several known, qualitative features of the neurogenic niche, such as blood vessel density and tortuosity. In some cases, we reproduce qualitative observations, such as affirming that vessel density is high in the subgranular zone (SGZ) where NSCs reside and low in the granule cell layer. In other cases, our findings go counter to what qualitative observations suggest. For example, the SGZ is often described as having uniquely linear blood vessels, but we found that linearity was similar between the SGZ and hilus layer. We also report new measures of features of DG layer vascular architecture: vessel diameter and branching. Together, these findings offer a global, quantitative characterization of the DG vascular niche in adult mice. Beyond providing more detailed characterization of DG vasculature, we also anticipate our methods and estimates of variance in mice will be useful for investigators wishing to plan their own quantitative studies of changes in the vascular structure of the DG.

items.title: Self-initiated restrictive feeding: a new mouse model of restrictive eating disorders
items.abstract_or_text: Restrictive eating disorders are serious psychiatric illnesses carrying the highest morality of any mental health condition, yet their neurobiology remains poorly understood. Progress is constrained by a shortage of animal models with convincing construct validity. In particular, anorexia nervosa (AN), a self-initiated restriction of caloric intake, is notoriously difficult to replicate in mice, which would otherwise offer an ideal pathway to understanding the neural mechanisms of this strongly gene-linked disorder, similar to advances in other neuropsychiatric conditions. Here, we introduce a model of self-initiated restrictive feeding (SIRF), using open-source behavioural devices. We show that SIRF specifically affects female mice, persists in the absence of the initial triggering conditions, and correlates with social rank - features that parallel AN. Meal pattern analysis shows that SIRF arises alongside decreased meal size and duration, with meal frequency unaltered in the long-term. Chemogenetic inhibition of the insular cortex, a brain region consistently implicated in AN and interoceptive processing, reduced SIRF. In sum, this proof-of-principle study suggests that SIRF provides a tractable model of self-initiated restriction as a platform for dissecting the neural circuits that initiate and sustain restrictive eating.

items.title: An integrative cardio-informatics approach identifies positionally conserved ancestors of human lncRNA genes transcribed across vertebrate hearts
items.abstract_or_text: The poor conservation of lncRNA genes limits their comprehensive functional studies, as genetic engineering of relevant animal models presupposes the presence of corresponding defined orthologs. This limitation is prominently evident in cardiovascular research, where heart-related lncRNAs are rarely conserved between humans and other vertebrates, despite the highly conserved nature of cardiac function. Because lncRNAs frequently regulate neighboring protein-coding genes essential for cardomyocyte function (herein termed cardiomyocyte indispensable, CMIs), we hypothesized that they are under evolutionary pressure to retain their genomic position and transcriptional activity, irrespective of sequence similarities to prototypical human lncRNA genes. By integrating mouse cardiac knockout phenotypes with human single-cell transcriptomics data, we systematically identified heart-expressed CMIs and their neighboring. lncRNA genes. Cross-species synteny analyses revealed regions flanking 109 CMIs with conserved relative positions and transcriptional orientations across vertebrate genomes. As most of these loci reside within poorly annotated non-coding regions, we developed VertLncRNAchecker, a neural network-based web interface, that predicts lncRNA-like genes within these regions, which we termed positional ancestors. Finally, we validated in situ that these positional ancestors express mature lncRNA transcripts in the hearts of mice, pigs, and frogs, mirroring the expression of their human lncRNA counterparts. We present an accurate and retrainable computational platform for cross-species lncRNA discovery that prioritizes conserved genomic position over sequence conservation or existing genome annotations. This pipeline revealed putative ancestors of human heart-related lncRNAs hidden within the vertebrate non-coding dark genome, providing novel insights into lncRNA biology and evolution.
